name: Wrenchtime
tagline: Job clock and labor time tracking built around wrench time for mechanics and maintenance crews.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: At its core this is a stopwatch attached to a job record, and a coding agent will give you that in an afternoon: jobs, techs, start/stop, a wrench time percentage, a weekly report. The hard part was never the timer, it is getting a greasy-handed person to actually hit start on a phone in a loud bay, then reconciling that against work orders and payroll. A personal or one-shop version is genuinely fine if you are the only one using it or you trust your crew to tap buttons. The moment you need offline mobile, multi-site rollups, or a handoff into a real maintenance or shop management system, the DIY version starts leaking. Public detail on this product is thin, so treat the verdict as directional rather than a teardown.
coreLoopDIY: A local web app where you pick a job and a tech, start and stop a timer, tag the interval as wrench time or waiting, and get a per-job and per-week breakdown you can export.
requirements: A machine or cheap VPS to run it on
A phone browser for the shop floor, ideally on the same network
Someone willing to enforce the clock-in habit
whatYouLose: A real mobile app that survives bad shop wifi and works offline
Multi-tech, multi-site rollups and manager dashboards that someone else maintains
Integrations into work order, parts, or payroll systems
Audit-safe time records if anyone ever disputes labor hours
Whatever benchmarking or canned reporting the paid product ships with
moatNotes: Labor time data gets ugly to migrate once payroll and job costing depend on it, and the integrations into shop or CMMS systems are the part nobody wants to rebuild.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because the product is not the timer, it is the discipline around the timer. Paying means someone else owns the mobile app that works in a dead zone, the reports a plant manager will actually read, and the record you can point at when a customer argues about billed hours. A shop owner replacing this with a self-hosted side project also becomes the person who gets called when the clock stops mid-shift, and that call always arrives at the worst time.
notes: The timer is trivial; the behavior change is not. Budget your effort accordingly.
prompt:
Build a self-hosted labor time tracker for a small repair shop or maintenance crew. Call it Wrenchclock.

Stack, no substitutions:
- Next.js 15 App Router, TypeScript, Tailwind. SQLite via better-sqlite3, file at ./data/wrenchclock.db, migrations run on boot.
- No auth provider, no cloud, no telemetry, no analytics. Single shared instance on a LAN.
- One env var in .env: APP_PIN, a shared numeric PIN checked by middleware and stored in a signed cookie. That is the entire security model, say so in the README.

Data model:
- techs: id, name, active.
- jobs: id, title, customer, vehicle_or_asset, status (open/closed), created_at.
- entries: id, job_id, tech_id, started_at, ended_at nullable, kind (wrench | waiting | parts | travel), note.

Screens:
- /clock: the only screen that matters. Big touch targets. Pick tech, pick job, pick kind, one huge Start/Stop button. Show the running timer and today's total for that tech. Must be usable one-handed on a phone browser.
- /jobs: list and create jobs, open a job to see all entries, total hours, and wrench time percentage (wrench minutes divided by all logged minutes).
- /reports: date range picker, per-tech and per-job totals, wrench time percentage, CSV export.
- /admin: add and deactivate techs, close jobs, manually edit or insert an entry with a required reason note.

Rules:
- A tech can only have one open entry; starting a new one auto-stops the previous and logs that it was auto-stopped.
- Never delete entries, soft-delete with a voided flag so edits stay visible in the job view.
- Durations computed from timestamps, never stored as totals.

Out of scope, do not build: invoicing, parts inventory, payroll export, native apps, offline sync, multi-tenant accounts, charts beyond simple bars.

Seed the database with three techs and four jobs so the UI is not empty. Include a README with setup, the PIN caveat, and a one-line SQLite backup command.
